historical_timeline.summary: High blood pressure; physicians advise rest; normal by May.
Blood pressure 194/130; ECG and oscillograph the next two days.
Fast at Rajkot with blood pressure up to 180/110, swelling of the feet, and acetone in the urine.
Basal metabolic test: height 5 feet 5 inches, weight 46.7 kg.
Writes that his blood pressure remains high and records his own readings.
Last fast, his eighteenth, at 78; kidney function reported impaired; broken on the sixth day.

claims.statement: Mahatma Gandhi was born on October 2, 1869.

According to his health file for 1924 to 1947, kept at the National Gandhi Museum, his blood pressure readings were as high as 194/130 on October 26, 1937, and 220/110 on February 19, 1940, and other readings in between reached about 170/110 and 180/105.

source_links.locator: Interesting facts of Mahatma Gandhi's health
Blood pressure; blood pressure profile table

claims.statement: In March 1927 his blood pressure was high throughout the day, and physicians' statements published in the Bombay Chronicle of March 29, 1927, warned of a danger of apoplexy from high blood pressure due to continuous overwork and advised absolute rest in a cool climate; on May 2, 1927, his blood pressure was found to be normal.

To lower his blood pressure he placed a mud poultice on his abdomen, applied a mud bandage to his head in summer, and took sarpagandha, an Ayurvedic preparation of Rauwolfia serpentina; a physician's account says he took garlic daily after it was suggested as a remedy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Rauwolfia serpentina is the source of reserpine, an old antihypertensive drug.

claims.statement: His electrocardiogram and oscillograph reports of October 27 and 28, 1937, found diminished arterial elasticity, a fairly good myocardium, and slight enlargement of the heart; the report of February 19, 1940, found slight myocarditis, normal for his age, with cardiovascular degeneration arrested.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Period terminology is reported as written; it does not map exactly to modern diagnoses.

source_links.locator: Condition of the heart; remarks on ECG and oscillograph

claims.statement: A basal metabolic test on April 30, 1939, recorded his height as 5 feet 5 inches and his weight as 46.7 kg.
claims.clinical_interpretation: These figures give a body mass index of about 17; press reports of a BMI of 17.1 appear to come from the basal metabolic rate of 17.1 printed on the same test.

claims.statement: During a fast at Rajkot in March 1939, health bulletins reported his blood pressure as 170/110 on March 4 with weakness of the heart and swelling of the feet, and 180/110 on March 5, with a loss of two pounds; a urine test on March 5 showed acetone in large amounts; he broke the fast on the afternoon of March 7 with fruit juices, honey, and jaggery.

In a letter of October 28, 1941, to one of his physicians, he wrote that his blood pressure continued to remain high, that he had taken three drops of sarpagandha morning and evening, and that his pressure was 166/98 that morning, 196/112 after talking while walking, and 150/90 in the afternoon, and that his food intake was good.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own measurements show the effect of activity on blood pressure.

claims.statement: He kept a vegetarian diet; he took a vow not to drink cow's or buffalo milk and later, when ill, accepted goat's milk on medical advice; in Key to Health he wrote that experience had taught him that a vegetarian diet must include milk and milk products such as curd, butter, and ghee.

source_links.locator: Interesting facts of Mahatma Gandhi's health

claims.statement: Earlier illnesses in the cited summary include pleurisy in London in 1914, acute dysentery in 1918 and 1929, an operation for piles in 1919, an operation for acute appendicitis on January 12, 1924, and malaria in 1925 and 1936.

He walked about 18 km a day for nearly 40 years, about 79,000 km during his campaigns from 1913 to 1948; his daily routine at Sevagram included a morning walk of about 5 km, kitchen and cleaning work, and spinning.

source_links.locator: Interesting facts of Mahatma Gandhi's health

claims.statement: Blood sugar measurements of 41 in January 1936, 71.4 in December 1937, and 115 in April 1938 are recorded in his health file; his cholesterol readings were within the normal range and his hemoglobin was 14.96 g/dL.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The very low 1936 value is reported as written; method and timing are not stated.

claims.statement: He preached against tea and coffee, along with drugs, tobacco, and alcohol.

source_links.locator: Interesting facts of Mahatma Gandhi's health

claims.statement: He began his last fast on January 13, 1948, at 78, his eighteenth fast; on its third day he was carried in an armchair, a bulletin on January 16 said his kidneys were not functioning properly, and he broke the fast on the sixth day.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Treat stage 2 hypertension in a thin, lacto-vegetarian 70-year-old man by the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline and the CMID schedule, choosing a drug and hold rules that suit a man who fasts; assess nutrition, protein, vitamin B12, vitamin D, and bone health within his diet; and, through shared decision-making that respects his fasting as an act of conscience, plan a seven-day fast and a NICE CG32 high-risk refeeding protocol (thiamine first, slow energy increase, prophylactic potassium, phosphate, and magnesium, and early electrolyte checks), with orthostatic checks and falls prevention throughout.

referral.question: Nutrition assessment for a 70-year-old lacto-vegetarian man with stage 2 hypertension, BMI 17.1, and vitamin B12 and D deficiency, who intends to keep a seven-day fast next month. Please assess his nutritional status, set energy and protein targets within his diet, advise on vitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium, sodium, and potassium, and write a safe plan for the fast and for refeeding that respects his decision to fast
referral.urgency: Soon, within four weeks and before the planned fast
referral.pertinent_history: Lifelong lacto-vegetarian by conviction, with goat's milk and curd, fruit, nuts, vegetables, and whole grains; no eggs, meat, fish, tea, coffee, or alcohol; little salt; walks 5 km daily; fasts for reasons of conscience. Stage 2 hypertension: 168/94 mmHg at intake, home average 162/92, ECG voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy; started amlodipine 2.5 mg; a thiazide avoided because of fasting and low weight. Weight 46.6 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 17.1; Mini Nutritional Assessment 20 (at risk). Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, MCV 99 fL, vitamin B12 238 pg/mL with methylmalonic acid 0.48 umol/L, folate 17.5 ng/mL, ferritin 46 ng/mL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 19 ng/mL, phosphate 3.4 and magnesium 2.0 mg/dL, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, eGFR 94. DXA ordered. He has full decision-making capacity and has decided to fast for seven days, taking water with a little salt and citrus juice
questions: What is his nutritional status, and does he meet criteria for malnutrition?
What energy and protein targets do you advise, and how can he meet them within his lacto-vegetarian diet with goat's milk?
How should vitamin B12, vitamin D, and calcium be managed, given his diet and his low bone mass risk?
What sodium and potassium advice fits his blood pressure and his diet?
What plan do you advise for the seven-day fast and for refeeding afterwards, given his refeeding risk?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Gandhi is seen at the request of Dr. Malhotra for nutrition assessment before a planned fast. He has eaten a lacto-vegetarian diet by conviction for most of his life and fasts from time to time for reasons of conscience; he wishes to fast for seven days from early April and asked for a plan to do so safely. A 24-hour recall and a three-day food record show three meals: goat's milk about 500 mL a day, curd, two whole-wheat flatbreads, boiled vegetables, a small serving of dal on some days, fruit, and a few nuts, with little added salt. Estimated intake is about 1350 kcal (29 kcal/kg) and 42 g of protein (0.9 g/kg) a day, calcium about 900 mg, sodium about 1200 mg, and vitamin B12 well under 1 mcg, since goat's milk contains little B12. His weight has been stable for years. He has no chewing or swallowing difficulty, no diarrhea, and no loss of appetite
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Intake weight, BMI, Mini Nutritional Assessment, blood count, vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, folate, ferritin, albumin, vitamin D, electrolytes, and kidney function; today's DXA and FRAX; the blood pressure plan and the amlodipine hold rules

exam.finding: Weight 46.4 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 17.0; weight stable over years by his report
Mild temporal and clavicular wasting; mild loss at the interosseous muscles of the hands and the quadriceps
Mild to moderate loss at the orbits and triceps
No edema or ascites
Left 22 kg, right 25 kg by dynamometer; below the 27 kg low-strength threshold for men
Tongue slightly smooth; skin, hair, and nails normal; own teeth, chewing well

assessment.display: Nutritional status: low BMI and reduced muscle mass without current malnutrition by GLIM
assessment.assessment: The phenotypic GLIM criteria are met (BMI below 22 at 70 or older and reduced muscle mass on examination and grip), but no etiologic criterion is met between fasts: intake meets his energy needs and there is no inflammatory disease. He is at risk (MNA 20). During a seven-day fast the reduced-intake criterion will be met, and after it he will be at high risk of refeeding problems by NICE criteria (BMI below 18.5 with little or no intake for more than five days). Nutrition diagnosis: inadequate protein intake related to limited protein foods in his chosen diet, as shown by about 0.9 g/kg a day against a need of 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg and low grip strength
Diet supplies well under the 2.4 mcg a day needed; goat's milk is a poor source. Food alone will not correct it, so a supplement is needed long term
Low vitamin D with calcium intake a little below target; relevant to his low bone mass
Calcium target 1000 to 1200 mg a day can be met with goat's milk and curd; protein adequacy also supports bone
Sodium about 1200 mg a day is already below 1500 mg; potassium from fruit and vegetables can be raised

recommendations: Energy about 30 kcal/kg a day (about 1400 kcal) and protein 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg a day (about 50 to 55 g), spread over three meals: add a bowl of curd, a daily serving of dal or chickpeas, and a handful of groundnuts or almonds, all within his diet

Vitamin B12 1 mg by mouth daily long term, as Dr. Malhotra has planned; vitamin D3 1000 units daily; calcium 1000 to 1200 mg a day from about 500 mL of goat's milk and two servings of curd, with sesame or leafy greens
Keep sodium below 1500 mg a day as now; raise potassium-rich fruit and vegetables, such as bananas, oranges, and lentils, since his kidney function is normal
During the fast: about 2 L a day of water with a pinch of salt and a little citrus juice, as he plans; rest and limit walking; daily home weight; the nurse's daily call

Refeeding, written plan: day 1 about 10 kcal/kg (about 440 kcal) in five or six small feeds of diluted fruit juice, goat's milk, curd, and rice gruel; increase by about 250 kcal a day to about 30 kcal/kg by days 5 to 7; protein back to 1.2 g/kg by day 7; fluids 30 to 35 mL/kg a day; thiamine before the first feed, a multivitamin and mineral tablet, and electrolyte supplements as prescribed
Electrolytes and weight before the first feed and daily for the first three days, then until stable, with daily dietitian calls to day 7
Recheck weight, Mini Nutritional Assessment, and food record in about three months
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Malhotra the same day. Mr. Gandhi took part in every decision; the plan works with his diet and his decision to fast rather than against them, and he was given the refeeding plan in writing
consultant_note.follow_up: Dietitian telephone calls daily from the first day of refeeding to day 7, then a review in about three months. Primary care manages blood pressure, laboratory monitoring, and supplements
